findings.paper_title: Report No.94.2026 - Financial Performance - Emerging Year Risk Managment
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing to long-term assets indicator improved from Red to Amber, showing positive movement in balance sheet health.
findings.detail: The fiscal indicator measuring long-term borrowing against long-term assets has moved from Red in the prior year to Amber in 2025/26, reflecting positive movement. This improvement reflects the council's early debt redemption strategy in response to changing interest rates. However, future capital investment decisions and borrowing affordability will continue to affect the revenue budget over the MTFS period.
findings.matters: Improving this indicator demonstrates the council is managing its balance sheet strategically and using the interest rate environment to reduce long-term liabilities. However, the prior Red rating indicates the council's historical debt position remains structurally challenging.
findings.figures: Prior year Red, 2025/26 Amber; long-term borrowing to tax revenue below comparator average (Green rating)
findings.quote: The long-term borrowing to long-term assets indicator has improved from Red to Amber, reflecting positive movement, but remains an area for attention as future capital investment, affordability of borrowing and the balance between internal and external financing will continue to affect the revenue budget over the MTFS period.

findings.paper_title: Report No.94.2026 - Financial Performance - Emerging Year Risk Managment
findings.headline: DSG/SEND funding pressures represent a significant medium-term sustainability risk despite current ringfencing from the General Fund.
findings.detail: The council faces increasing demand and complexity within SEND provision, pressuring the High Needs Block of the DSG. While DSG funding is ringfenced and does not currently impact the General Fund, national funding arrangements remain uncertain. Future changes to the statutory override could expose councils with significant DSG deficits to greater financial pressure, requiring General Fund support.
findings.matters: A material DSG deficit is a future liability. If the statutory override is removed or reformed, the council could face a significant budget shock. Even ringfenced, it signals an unsustainable service delivery model.
findings.figures: High risk, Increasing trend; funding status ringfenced but uncertain
findings.quote: The Council continues to face financial risk arising from increasing demand and complexity within Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) provision and the resulting pressure on the High Needs Block of the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG). Whilst DSG funding is ringfenced, national funding arrangements remain uncertain and future changes to the statutory override could place greater financial pressure on local authorities with significant DSG deficits.

findings.paper_title: Report No.94.2026 - Financial Performance - Emerging Year Risk Managment
findings.headline: Risk reserves of £6.9m are above strategy levels but face significant erosion if the £2.3m overspend continues to year-end.
findings.detail: The council holds £6.9m in risk reserves (£1.1m Budget Risk Reserve plus £5.787m Risk Reserve) intended to manage risk and support transformation, not to fund recurring service pressures. A full-year overspend at the Q1 rate would consume 33% of these reserves. The council acknowledges that continued overspends, savings slippage, or demand growth in social care could erode these balances and weaken financial resilience.
findings.matters: Reserves are the buffer against volatility. Drawing them down to cover recurring service pressures rather than one-off costs or transformation is unsustainable and signals underlying budgets are misaligned to actual demand.
findings.figures: Total risk reserves £6.9m; Q1 overspend £2.3m represents 33% of reserves if full-year outcome
findings.quote: Whilst reserves remain above strategy levels, continued drawdown at this scale would significantly reduce resilience and the Council's ability to manage future demand-led pressures.

findings.paper_title: Report No.94.2026 - Financial Performance - Emerging Year Risk Managment
findings.headline: Investment returns outperformed benchmark by 50 basis points at 4.24%, demonstrating effective cash management within approved limits.
findings.detail: The council's treasury position remains stable with all prudential indicators on target. Investment returns of 4.24% exceed the SONIA benchmark of 3.74% by 50 basis points, reflecting deployment of short-term investments at higher rates. The council remains underborrowed (£4.7m below the underlying borrowing requirement), external borrowing is within approved limits, and treasury strategy compliance is full.
findings.matters: Strong investment returns provide a financial buffer and reduce borrowing pressure. This demonstrates competent cash management and improves overall treasury resilience during a period of demand-driven overspends.
findings.figures: Investment returns 4.24% vs benchmark 3.74% (50bps outperformance); underborrowed position £4.7m
findings.quote: The Council outperformed the benchmark by 50bps, demonstrating the Council has been investing excess balances to maximise returns but still investing within the Boundaries of the Investment Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Report No.94.2026 - Financial Performance - Emerging Year Risk Managment
findings.headline: Capital programme spending is significantly behind forecast: £1.9m actual against £6.3m profiled, with three projects requesting budget slippage.
findings.detail: The council has spent only £1.9m of the £6.3m profiled capital spend at quarter 1. Three named projects have requested budget slippage: Melton Local Regeneration Fund (£2.3m), Public Realm Strategy (£0.6m), and Disabled Facility Grants (£0.3m). Finance and the Project Management Office are working to align delivery risks and reporting.
findings.matters: Sustained capital underspend signals delivery or procurement capacity constraints and can delay service improvements and revenue savings. It also affects treasury planning if councils have borrowed expecting to spend.
findings.figures: £1.9m actual spend vs £6.3m profiled; Melton LRF £2.3m slippage; Public Realm £0.6m; Disabled Facility Grants £0.3m
findings.quote: Profiling of the capital programme continues to be a risk on the Capital Programme with spend of £1.9m against profiled spend of £6.3m.

findings.paper_title: Report No.94.2026 - Financial Performance - Emerging Year Risk Managment
findings.headline: Adult social care demand exceeds forecast across both older people and working-age cohorts, with financial impact currently unquantified.
findings.detail: Adult social care is flagged as high-risk with an increasing trend. Both older people homecare and working-age adults cohorts are generating demand greater than forecast, with costs marked as unknown. The council is implementing mitigation strategies including block bed contracts, review panels, and expansion of internal provision, but the underlying demand pressure is growing.
findings.matters: Adult social care overspends typically indicate demographic or service complexity trends that will persist. Inability to control costs in this area signals structural budget misalignment and creates ongoing pressure on reserves.
findings.figures: High risk, Increasing trend; cost impact Unknown
findings.quote: Demand greater than forecast position. This risk relates to both the Older People and Working Age Adults cohorts.

findings.paper_title: Report No.94.2026 - Financial Performance - Emerging Year Risk Managment
findings.headline: Quarter 1 revenue overspend of £2.3m, equivalent to 4.1% of net budget, driven by demand-led services across adult social care, children's services, waste, planning and transport.
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £2.3m overspend at quarter 1. Management action has mitigated approximately 53% of the gross risk exposure, reducing identified pressures from £4.9m. If the overspend persists to year-end without further mitigation, it would consume approximately 33% of the council's identified risk reserves (£6.9m).
findings.matters: An in-year overspend of this scale indicates demand management issues and erodes the council's financial resilience. Drawing reserves to cover recurring service pressures rather than transformation or one-off events is unsustainable.
findings.figures: £2.3m overspend; 4.1% of net revenue budget; gross risk exposure £4.9m; management mitigation £2.6m (53%); would represent 33% of risk reserves
findings.quote: At Quarter 1 the Council is forecasting a £2.3m overspend (4.1% of net revenue budget), driven primarily by demand-led services across Adult Social Care, Children's Services, Waste Management, Planning and Transport.

findings.headline: Multiple prior year audit recommendations remain unaddressed or incompletely implemented after 12 months
findings.detail: From 6 recommendations in the 2024/25 audit findings, management has fully addressed only 1–2 items. User access review processes only commenced in April 2026 (after the audit period) with no evidence of review taking place during 2025/26. Related party completeness review using Companies House searches has not been undertaken. Data classification policy remains in scoping phase with initial meeting only in Q3 2026.
findings.matters: Slow implementation of audit recommendations indicates the council's capacity or willingness to address identified control weaknesses, affecting overall governance maturity and financial control quality.
findings.figures: 2 of 6 prior recommendations fully or substantially addressed; 3 noted as 'not yet addressed'
findings.quote: Management provided a user access listing dated May 2026, described as evidence that a review of user access had taken place. However, the evidence provided did not demonstrate that an actual review had been performed... We were also informed that the access review process only commenced in April 2026, indicating that no such review was in operation for the remainder of the 2025/26 period under audit.

findings.headline: Council not complying with new 2025/26 Code requirement for 5-year rolling PPE revaluations supported by annual indexation
findings.detail: The 2025/26 Code introduced a requirement for property, plant and equipment to be revalued on a 5-year rolling basis with annual indexation in intervening years. Rutland is continuing with its previous 3-year rolling revaluation programme and has not indexed assets not revalued in year. Audit testing found no material valuation issues and management's assessment that indexation impact would be immaterial was considered reasonable, so the 2025/26 statements are not materially misstated.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with current accounting standards represents a technical audit finding; if the council does not transition to the compliant approach, future year indexation calculations risk omitting deferred movements.
findings.figures: Land and buildings valuation £20.8m
findings.quote: From our PPE work we identified that the Authority's approach to revaluation and indexation does not comply with the Code. The Code changes for 2025/26 include a revaluation expedient for PPE, requiring valuations once every five years, or on a five-year rolling basis, supported by indexation in the intervening years. The Authority has continued with its three-year rolling revaluation programme.

findings.headline: Audit work on £141.6m gross pension liability remains incomplete pending pension fund auditor assurance
findings.detail: The valuation of the LGPS pension liability of £141.6m represents a significant accounting estimate due to its size, complexity, and sensitivity to actuarial assumptions including discount rate, inflation, salary growth, and life expectancy. The council's auditors are dependent on receiving assurance from the pension fund's own auditors; this work was still outstanding at the time the audit findings were reported.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities typically represent the largest contingent obligation for local authorities and are highly sensitive to assumption changes; incomplete audit work delays final assurance and represents a key contingency for financial reporting.
findings.figures: £141.6m gross LGPS liability at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The valuation of the gross pension fund liability represents a significant estimate due to its size, complexity and sensitivity to changes in key assumptions. At 31 March 2026, the LGPS liability was £141,6 million... Our work in this area is incomplete, subject to a response from the pension fund auditor which is due shortly.

findings.headline: Journal approval process remains email-based rather than system-controlled, a repeat finding in its third consecutive year
findings.detail: Auditors have identified for the third consecutive year (2023/24, 2024/25, 2025/26) that journal approvals are undertaken via email rather than directly within the Agresso system. This creates an opportunity for journals to be posted without approval and edited after approval has been given. Management acknowledges limited finance team resources create practical constraints in implementing system-based approval, and considers compensating controls sufficient. Audit testing identified no instances of journals posted without approval.
findings.matters: Persistent control weaknesses over journal processing increase the risk of unauthorized or fraudulent entries that could misstate the financial statements, and the third repetition suggests implementation capacity constraints.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: This is a repeat observation, having previously been raised in 2023/24 and 2024/25. Management has acknowledged that the Authority's finance team operates with limited resources, creating practical constraints in implementing the recommendation to approve journals directly within the Agresso system.

findings.headline: Council's going concern disclosure should be updated to reflect government's decision to pause the Local Government Reorganisation programme
findings.detail: The council has included a significant going concern disclosure in the financial statements, but this should be updated to reflect the government's recent announcement that the LGR programme is being paused and reviewed. LGR has major strategic implications for the council's future operating model, structure, and funding arrangements.
findings.matters: LGR was a material strategic initiative; its pause creates fundamental uncertainty about the council's future that should be clearly disclosed to users assessing financial sustainability and viability.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: The Authority have included a significant disclosure in the accounts in relation to going concern, this should be updated to reflect the Government's recent announcement that the LGR programme is being paused and reviewed.

findings.headline: Community Infrastructure Levy incorrectly classified as creditor rather than reserve, increasing stated usable reserves by £6.378m
findings.detail: CIL receipts totalling £6.378m (£5.361m at 31 March 2025 and £1.017m in 2025/26) were misclassified as short-term creditors when they should have been held as earmarked reserves. This requires prior period adjustment restating 2024/25 comparatives and creation of a third balance sheet as at 1 April 2024. While this is a balance sheet reclassification with no impact on underlying cash position, it significantly improves the stated reserve position.
findings.matters: Reserve levels are key indicators of financial sustainability and resilience that lenders use to assess financial strength; a material restatement affecting reserves warrants scrutiny of underlying controls.
findings.figures: £6.378m cumulative adjustment (£5.361m prior year, £1.017m current year)
findings.quote: CIL receipts were incorrectly recognised as short-term creditors rather than as income transferred to Capital Grants Unapplied. Correcting this increases net assets and usable reserves by £5.361m at 31 March 2025 (£1.626m through the FY24/25 CIES, £3.735m as an opening reserves adjustment) and a further £1.017m in 2025/26 — £6.378m cumulatively.

findings.headline: Auditors anticipate unmodified opinion on financial statements
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's audit work is substantially complete with no identified matters that would require modification of the audit opinion. The auditors expect to issue an unmodified audit opinion on 6 October 2026, indicating the financial statements present a true and fair view in accordance with applicable accounting standards and legal requirements.
findings.matters: An unmodified audit opinion provides assurance on the reliability and accuracy of the financial statements that lenders and finance directors rely on when assessing the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Opinion anticipated 6 October 2026
findings.quote: Our anticipated financial statements audit report opinion will be unmodified. We anticipate issuing the auditors report on 6 October.

findings.paper_title: Report No.102.2026 - Statement of Account & External Auditors Annual Audit Report 2025.26
findings.headline: Rutland was one of only ten councils to publish accounts by the original statutory deadline.
findings.detail: While the deadline was extended (allowing 85% of unitary authorities to publish eventually), Rutland published by the original 31 May 2026 deadline with only 9 other councils, and is likely to be among the first to publish audited accounts. This indicates efficient financial processes and effective audit relationships.
findings.matters: Timely publication of audited accounts indicates strong financial management capability and effective internal control processes. It also means lenders and stakeholders get financial assurance sooner.
findings.figures: 10 councils published by 31 May 2026; 85% by extended deadline
findings.quote: It is likely that Rutland will be one of the first authorities to publish an audited set of accounts.

findings.detail: Grant Thornton charged £9,000 in fee variations against the published scale fee of £231,583. Of these, £3,000 related to 'overrun on the property, plant and equipment work due to delays in response and the quality of evidence provided.' This suggests documentation or evidence-gathering issues.
findings.matters: Fee overruns due to evidence quality and response delays indicate potential gaps in record-keeping or documentation practices. Combined with the PPE recommendation above, this suggests asset management processes warrant strengthening.

findings.headline: The council maintained financial reserves and balanced its budget despite growing SEND demand and sector-wide pressures.
findings.detail: Officers confirm the council 'demonstrates good financial stewardship, maintaining reserves and balancing the budget despite growing service demand pressures.' This shows effective financial management even while facing the DSG deficit pressures noted above.
findings.matters: Reserve maintenance and budget balance are key indicators of financial resilience and prudent management. They show the council can absorb future shocks without requiring emergency funding or unplanned borrowing.

This represents the strongest possible audit assurance on financial position and governance.

findings.paper_title: Report No.102.2026 - Statement of Account & External Auditors Annual Audit Report 2025.26
findings.headline: DSG deficit and SEND-related financial pressures remain the council's main ongoing financial risk.
findings.detail: The external auditor identifies the DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit and SEND-related costs as the main issue requiring continued oversight. Auditors acknowledge the council has strengthened its oversight, governance, and planning arrangements around these issues, suggesting active management, but the pressure itself remains unresolved.
findings.matters: DSG deficits represent demand-led financial pressures that can significantly impact financial sustainability. Lenders need to know whether such material pressures are being managed effectively.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the paper
findings.quote: The main issue requiring continued senior oversight remains the DSG deficit and SEND-related financial pressure.

findings.headline: EHCP assessments completed within statutory timescale at only 18% against national target of 90%, representing material underperformance of statutory duty.
findings.detail: The Council is failing to meet statutory targets for issuing Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) within 20 weeks of request. Performance at year-end was 18% against the national target of 90%. The auditor's review found that while the Council uses detailed Power BI dashboards enabling close monitoring of the EHCP process, performance remained off-track at year-end despite Q2 mitigating actions. The auditor also identified a reconciliation issue between figures reported to members and those published on GOV.UK, which the Council is investigating. The auditor notes there is no indication of an issue with the Council's own data, but external benchmarking could have identified the discrepancy earlier.
findings.matters: Material underperformance of a statutory duty creates legal and reputational risk, may expose the Council to challenge, and indicates either resource constraints or service design problems that require resolution.
findings.figures: EHCP performance 18% against 90% target; FOI performance improved from 39.5% (Q2) to 100% (June 2026).
findings.quote: year end performance was 18% against the national target of 90%

findings.headline: Adult Social Care and Children's Services reporting in-year overspends of £1.7 million and £0.3 million respectively, reflecting demand and cost pressures in statutory services.
findings.detail: The Council continues to face significant pressures within its statutory social care services. The Adults and Health Directorate reported a £1.7 million overspend, and Children and Families reported a £0.3 million overspend, both driven by increases in demand, complexity and cost. These were offset by underspends in other areas (Places £1.6 million, Corporate Costs £0.7 million, Law and Governance £0.2 million), resulting in the overall £0.7 million revenue underspend. The auditor notes that the pressures experienced by Rutland are representative of the national picture, suggesting these are not one-off issues.
findings.matters: Ongoing structural overspends in statutory services signal unsustainable cost pressures that cannot be offset indefinitely by underspends in discretionary areas, and indicate services may be operating below service quality thresholds.
findings.figures: Adults and Health overspend £1.7 million; Children and Families overspend £0.3 million; offset by Places underspend £1.6 million, Corporate Costs £0.7 million, Law and Governance £0.2 million; overall revenue underspend £0.7 million.
findings.quote: The Council reported a £0.7 million underspend against its £56.8 million net revenue budget in 2025/26. This was achieved despite ongoing increases in demand, complexity and cost in social care services. Key cost pressures included a £1.7 million overspend within the Adults and Health Directorate, and £0.3 million in Children and Families.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation currently paused for review following government announcement on 7 September 2026.
findings.detail: In July 2026, the government approved reorganisation proposals for Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland, with Rutland planned to merge into a new unitary council. However, following a government announcement on 7 September 2026, the reorganisation is now paused for review. During 2025/26, governance structures were developed in preparation for the expected reorganisation. The auditor notes that risks will remain once LGR transition recommences, including: programme management and governance with other demising councils; disaggregation and aggregation of services and finances; maintaining financial systems and hosting arrangements; ensuring stewardship and best value compliance during transition; and managing residual service and financial risks.
findings.matters: The pause creates strategic uncertainty about the Council's future governance structure, scale, and service delivery arrangements, which could affect its financial planning and operational continuity. Risks remain significant once implementation resumes.
findings.figures: Reorganisation approval July 2026; pause announced 7 September 2026.
findings.quote: reorganisation across Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland is currently paused for review

findings.headline: Reserves above average at £27.2 million (48% of net revenue expenditure) but forecast to decline sharply from £25.7 million in 2026/27 to £13.15 million in 2028/29.
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2026, the Council held total reserves of £27.2 million, which was £1.4 million higher than planned and above the mean level maintained by English unitary authorities. However, the Medium-Term Financial Strategy forecasts earmarked reserves declining from £25.7 million in 2026/27 to £13.15 million in 2028/29 (a decline of 49%), while the general fund reserve is forecast to remain at £3 million. This sharp decline in reserves capacity, combined with growing DSG deficits and service pressures, reduces the Council's financial buffer for unplanned events.
findings.matters: While current reserves are strong, their rapid planned depletion combined with uncertain DSG funding and growing service deficits will significantly reduce financial flexibility and resilience by 2028/29.
findings.figures: Total reserves £27.2 million at 31 March 2026; earmarked reserves forecast £25.7 million (2026/27) declining to £13.15 million (2028/29); general fund reserve forecast £3 million; new harmonisation reserve £0.371 million.
findings.quote: earmarked reserves are expected to decrease from the forecast £25.7 million in 2026/27 to £13.15 million in 2028/29

findings.headline: Auditor issued unqualified opinion on financial statements with no statutory recommendations or adverse powers used.
findings.detail: The Council received an unqualified audit opinion on its financial statements for 2025/26. The auditor identified two material adjustments of a classification nature (which also impacted prior year balances), and a small number of other adjustments that did not have material impact on year-end balances. The Council did not receive any written statutory recommendations, court applications, judicial review applications, or Public Interest Reports. However, the audit was affected by valuation evidence issues relating to a change in external valuer and untimely internal information provision, requiring formal escalation and audit overruns.
findings.matters: An unqualified opinion and absence of statutory powers used is positive assurance on accounts quality, but audit overruns and evidence issues flag potential control weaknesses in asset valuation and finance team capacity.
findings.figures: Two material classification adjustments identified; audit opinion unqualified; draft accounts published 29 May 2026.
findings.quote: We intend to issue an unqualified opinion on the Council's financial statements shortly after the Audit and Risk Committee.

findings.headline: Savings delivery shortfall: Council achieved £2.2 million of £3.1 million planned savings target (71%), with £0.9 million undelivered.
findings.detail: The Council failed to deliver 29% of its planned savings programme in 2025/26. The shortfall was driven primarily by a £0.3 million variance relating to pay award assumptions, where the final pay award of 3.2% exceeded the 2% increase budgeted. At Q1 2026/27, the Council has identified £6.6 million of new savings and reported that 86% were either completed or in progress, suggesting improved momentum but also indicating that savings remain a structural challenge.
findings.matters: Recurring inability to deliver planned savings suggests either over-optimistic planning or operational constraints, both of which carry risk for future budget balance and may require service reductions or reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: £2.2 million delivered against £3.1 million target (71% achievement); £0.9 million shortfall; £6.6 million identified for 2026/27 with 86% completed or in progress at Q1.
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the Council delivered £2.2 million of savings against a target of £3.1 million, achieving 71% of the planned savings programme.

findings.headline: Cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reached £10.1 million at 31 March 2026, with forecast to reach £20.9 million by March 2028.
findings.detail: The Council reported an in-year DSG deficit of £4.2 million in 2025/26, increasing the cumulative deficit to £10.1 million. The Council expects government support via the High Needs Stability Grant (HNSG) of approximately £9.1 million (90% of the cumulative deficit), but this is subject to approval and conditions not yet confirmed. The Council has set aside £2.4 million in reserves to fund the remaining 10% contribution once the statutory override ends in March 2028. However, the deficit is forecast to grow to £15.7 million in 2026/27 and £20.9 million in 2027/28, creating risk that the reserve provision will prove insufficient and that government support for deficits beyond 2025/26 may not materialize.
findings.matters: A growing contingent liability and pressure on reserves that could constrain the Council's financial flexibility and medium-term strategy if government support does not materialise or if demand continues to exceed projections.
findings.figures: In-year deficit £4.2 million, cumulative deficit £10.1 million (31 March 2026), forecast £15.7 million (2026/27) and £20.9 million (2027/28); expected HNSG grant £9.1 million; Council reserve provision £2.4 million.
findings.quote: the Council continues to experience pressure on its DSG budgets, reporting an in-year DSG deficit of £4.2 million, increasing the cumulative deficit to £10.1 million at the end of 2025/26

The council's control framework for information requests has identified gaps that pose medium risk to delivery of objectives.

findings.detail: National pay negotiations with unions are ongoing with unions having rejected the latest offer. The council's 2026/27 budget assumption is 3% pay award, but the current offer being negotiated is higher than this. This risk is rated red with unknown cost impact. If a settlement above 3% is reached, there will be additional pay cost pressure beyond budget.
findings.matters: Pay is the largest cost base in the council and a settlement higher than 3% would generate additional overspend pressure across all directorates.
findings.figures: 3% budgeted, actual offer higher (amount unknown)
findings.quote: National pay negotiations continue with Unions rejecting the latest offer. The Council assumption was 3%, with the current offer being higher than this.

findings.headline: Homelessness costs carry uncompensated burden due to housing benefit subsidy rules
findings.detail: The Resources directorate is carrying a red-rated risk that housing benefits are subject to complex subsidy rules, with some homelessness-related costs not fully recoverable from government. This creates a structural budget pressure where the council bears part of the cost of homelessness services without corresponding government funding. Mitigation is limited to minimising length of stays in temporary accommodation.
findings.matters: An uncompensated cost burden in homelessness services, where the council bears costs that government subsidy rules do not cover, represents a structural revenue pressure driven by national policy.
findings.figures: Red-rated risk with cost range £0-£100k estimated
findings.quote: Housing benefits are subject to complex subsidy rules, with some homelessness-related costs not fully recoverable from Government.

findings.headline: Melton Local Regeneration Fund project slipping £2.3m with key planning and lease dependencies unresolved
findings.detail: The Melton Town Centre LRF project (part of the £12.2m total LRF programme) is forecasting £2.3m expenditure slippage into future years. The council is undertaking affordability work, value engineering, and revisions to delivery strategy following contractor estimates exceeding the construction budget. Key project dependencies including planning matters, access arrangements, lease arrangements, and procurement approvals remain unresolved before the main construction contract can be awarded.
findings.matters: Material slippage on a major regeneration project with key uncertainties (planning, lease terms) still pending indicates delivery risk and potential for further delays or cost overruns.
findings.figures: £2.3m Melton LRF slippage (of £12.2m total project), £3.2m total capital slippage across programme
findings.quote: key project dependencies, including planning matters, access and lease arrangements, and procurement approvals, remain to be resolved before the main construction contract can be awarded.

findings.headline: Demand Responsive Transport service has unresolved £0.2m funding gap with business case still under development
findings.detail: Public Transport DRT service is forecasting a £0.2m funding gap on the council's budget. The service is reviewing mitigation options and developing a business case to reassess the assumptions underpinning the DRT service model. This is one of the four red-rated savings plans (DRT contributions assumed additional external funding that has not materialised). No resolution is expected by Q1 forecast date and further information is promised for Q2.
findings.matters: An unresolved £0.2m funding gap in a service where assumptions about external contributions have failed suggests either the service model is unaffordable or external funding commitments are not materially available.
findings.figures: £0.2m funding gap on DRT
findings.quote: Public Transport is currently forecasting a funding gap of £0.2m on the DRT service. The service is reviewing options to mitigate this pressure and is developing a business case to reassess the assumptions underpinning the Demand Responsive Transport (DRT) service.

findings.headline: Waste services facing £190k DMR overspend from contractor facility fire and disposal costs inflation
findings.detail: Dry Mixed Recycling is forecasting £190k overspend due to a fire at the current contractor's facility requiring material to be diverted to an alternative processing site at higher cost. Household Waste Recycling Centre disposal costs are up £131k due to increased volumes. Green waste income is down £89k due to subscription numbers being lower than budgeted despite a price increase. Services are reviewing efficiency and procurement arrangements but the pressures are material.
findings.matters: Waste is a demand-driven service exposed to contractor market conditions, price inflation, and income volatility; this Q1 position shows multiple cost pressures that may persist.
findings.figures: £190k DMR overspend, £131k disposal overspend, £89k green waste income shortfall
findings.quote: Dry Mixed Recycling (DMR) is forecast to overspend by £190k at Quarter 1 due to higher processing costs following a fire at the current contractor's facility, requiring material to be diverted to an alternative processing site.

findings.headline: Planning fee income shortfall due to reformed fee regime capped at 90% cost recovery
findings.detail: Planning is forecast to overspend by £0.2m due to income shortfall. The budget assumed full cost recovery following introduction of fee reform from April 2027, but legislation has now been confirmed to commence December 2026 at only 90% of cost recovery, not full recovery. Planning application volumes remain subdued nationally. This is one of four red-rated savings plans and the service is taking a prudent view of income for the remainder of the year.
findings.matters: A policy change limiting fee recovery to 90% rather than full cost recovery represents a permanent reduction in the council's income capacity from this service.
findings.figures: £0.2m overspend forecast, 90% cost recovery vs full recovery, reform begins December 2026
findings.quote: the anticipated introduction of legislation allowing local authorities to set their own planning fees. At the point of forecast the legislation was expected to come in from April 2027. Since the forecast legislation has been confirmed at 90% of cost and will commence from December 2026.

findings.headline: Adult social care demand and cost inflation persisting despite internal provision expansion
findings.detail: Older people residential care is £0.6m over budget, driven by 7 additional service users (£0.4m pressure) and average cost premiums of £39 per week above budget assumptions. Working age adults are £0.5m over budget due to increased complexity and service users in mental health and learning disability placements. Homecare is £0.37m over due to 5 additional service users and travel costs. The council is using internal Day Opportunities and Supported Living provision to contain costs but demand continues to exceed budget, with further increases not yet factored into forecasts.
findings.matters: Sustained demand growth and cost inflation in adult social care despite the council's investment in internal provision suggests demographic or needs trends are outpacing budget assumptions.
findings.figures: £0.6m older people overspend, 7 additional service users, £39/week cost premium, £0.37m homecare overspend
findings.quote: Rising costs of care and support for Working Age Adults has led to a £0.5m pressure against planned budget mainly within Mental Health and Learning Disability residential care placements.

findings.headline: Four red-rated savings plans projected to deliver only £657k of £1.217m target (46% shortfall)
findings.detail: Of 34 savings plans totalling £6.563m target, four are rated red as falling short of target by more than 25% and with limited mitigation scope: garden & bulky waste (subscriptions below budget despite price increase), planning budget realignment (fee reform delayed and at only 90% cost recovery), highways & transport (demand and contract costs higher than expected), and DRT contributions (funding gap unresolved). Together these four red plans are forecast to achieve only £657k of their £1.217m target. Overall savings delivery forecast at £5.879m vs £6.563m (10.4% shortfall).
findings.matters: A 10% shortfall in planned savings, with four plans rated red and offering limited mitigation, indicates structural revenue challenges are not being resolved as planned, requiring either service cuts or further reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £1.217m red-rated target, £657k forecast (46% shortfall), total £5.879m vs £6.563m target
findings.quote: Saving forecast to fall short of target (over 25%) with limited scope of mitigation

findings.headline: £1.1m children's placements overspend driven by single high-cost placement not anticipated at budget setting
findings.detail: Children's placements are forecasting a £1.1m overspend at Q1 primarily driven by a new high-cost placement that was not in the budget assumptions. Additionally, the Children's Home was planned to open and begin offsetting placement costs and generating income, but implementation has been delayed past the original timeline, so those benefits will not materialise in 2026/27. Independent Fostering Agency and in-house fostering placements are also above budget due to higher activity and demand.
findings.matters: This demonstrates high volatility in children's services costs driven by individual high-need placements, with planned mitigation (the new children's home) now delayed, so savings are deferred into future years.
findings.figures: £1.1m overspend in placements, implementation delayed past initial plan
findings.quote: The children's placements budget is forecasting an overspend of £1.1m, primarily driven by a new high-cost placement that was not anticipated at the time the 2026/27 budget was set.

findings.headline: £2.3m revenue overspend at Q1 despite mitigation of 53% of identified pressures
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £2.3m overspend (4.1% of the £56.8m budget) even after successfully mitigating 53% of identified cost and demand pressures through management action, income generation, and service transformation. With nine months of the year remaining, the position indicates sustained underlying pressure from adult social care demand, children's placements, waste management, planning, and transport services that management action alone has not resolved.
findings.matters: A 4.1% overspend this early in the financial year, despite aggressive mitigation, signals demand and cost pressures may persist through the remainder of the year, putting reserves at risk.
findings.figures: £2.3m overspend, 4.1% of net revenue budget, 53% of pressures mitigated
findings.quote: At Quarter 1, the Council is forecasting an overspend of £2.3m against budget, equivalent to 4.1% of the net revenue budget.

findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit rising to £15.5m with no government confirmation on funding arrangements
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit for 2026/27 is forecast at £5.4m, bringing the accumulated deficit to £15.5m — equivalent to 10.1% of the council's entire net revenue budget. The council submitted a recovery plan to the Department for Education and is awaiting autumn approval announcement. Critically, government has not yet confirmed how DSG deficits will be funded for 2026/27 and 2027/28, leaving the council exposed to uncertainty about its future liability.
findings.matters: A £15.5m accumulated deficit represents a major financial burden the council must cashflow from reserves. Uncertainty about government funding arrangements for future years creates medium-term planning risk.
findings.figures: £15.5m accumulated deficit, £5.4m in-year deficit, 10.1% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: the Council continues to forecast expenditure materially above the grant received from Government and remains exposed to uncertainty regarding future national funding arrangements.

findings.headline: £1.217m of savings plans rated RED: forecast to fall short of target by over 25% with limited mitigation scope
findings.detail: Of the £6.563m medium-term savings target, four plans totalling £1.217m are rated RED as forecast to fall short by over 25% with limited mitigation. These include garden waste (subscription numbers below budget despite price increase), planning budget realignment (now dependent on delayed/reduced-recovery planning reform), highways and transport realignment (service forecasting overspends not savings), and DRT additional contributions (funding gap remains).
findings.matters: Multiple budgeted savings plans are failing to materialise. Combined with the Q1 overspend, this suggests the council is struggling to manage emerging cost and demand pressures and has hedged its budget on income/savings assumptions that are proving unreliable.
findings.figures: £1.217m in red-rated savings plans out of £6.563m total savings target; only £5.9m forecast achieved (89.9%)
findings.quote: Some savings remain at risk, notably those linked to planning fee reforms, transport services and additional income generation proposals.

findings.headline: Melton Local Regeneration Fund capital scheme slipping £2.3m due to contractor cost overruns requiring value engineering
findings.detail: The Melton LRF project (part of a £12.182m total LRF commitment) is forecast to slip £2.3m into future years. Slippage is driven by ongoing work to finalise construction affordability following contractor estimates that exceeded available budget. Key project dependencies including planning, access, lease arrangements and procurement approvals remain unresolved before main contract award.
findings.matters: A major capital scheme is running over budget at the design/procurement stage. Value engineering will be needed to bring costs back within available budget, and multiple project dependencies remain unresolved.
findings.figures: £2.3m slippage on £12.182m total Melton LRF project
findings.quote: The project is forecast to slip into future financial years due to ongoing work to finalise the construction affordability position, including value engineering and revisions to the delivery strategy following contractor estimates exceeding the available construction budget.

findings.headline: Demand Responsive Transport service £0.2m funding gap with business case under review for model sustainability
findings.detail: Public Transport is forecasting a £0.2m funding gap on the DRT service. This suggests the current operating model assumptions may not be sustainable and could require significant changes.
findings.matters: A business case review of an established service suggests current financial or operational viability concerns. This may foreshadow service redesign or reduced provision.
findings.figures: £0.2m funding gap on DRT service
findings.quote: Public Transport is currently forecasting a funding gap of £0.2m on the DRT service. The service is reviewing options to mitigate this pressure and is developing a business case to reassess the assumptions underpinning the Demand Responsive Transport (DRT) service.

findings.headline: Dry Mixed Recycling cost pressure of £190k from contractor facility fire requiring emergency diversion

This is compounded by Waste Disposal overspending by £131k from higher HWRC volumes. The council is progressing procurement and service review activity to address these pressures.
findings.matters: An operational disruption (contractor facility fire) is creating material unbudgeted costs. The council faces both this emergency pressure and structural waste volume increases, suggesting the waste service model may need restructuring.
findings.figures: £190k DMR overspend, £131k Waste Disposal overspend
findings.quote: Dry Mixed Recycling (DMR) is forecast to overspend by £190k at Quarter 1 due to higher processing costs following a fire at the current contractor's facility, requiring material to be diverted to an alternative processing site.

findings.headline: Planning fee income reform delivering 90% cost recovery instead of 100%, starting December 2026 not April 2027
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumed full cost recovery from planning fee reforms starting April 2027. Legislation has now been confirmed at 90% cost recovery starting December 2026. This is one of four savings plans rated RED as forecast to fall short of target by over 25% with limited mitigation scope. Planning application volumes also remain subdued nationally, creating Q1 overspend of £0.2m.
findings.matters: This is a budgeted savings/income plan that is now delivering materially less than anticipated. It demonstrates income assumption risk and failed budget realisations.
findings.figures: 90% recovery instead of full cost recovery; December 2026 start instead of April 2027; £0.2m Q1 overspend
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget assumed that full cost recovery would be achieved during the second half of the year following the anticipated introduction of legislation allowing local authorities to set their own planning fees. At the point of forecast the legislation was expected to come in from April 2027. Since the forecast legislation has been confirmed at 90% of cost and will commence from December 2026.

findings.headline: Children's placements overspending by £1.1m from single unanticipated high-cost placement
findings.detail: The placements budget is forecasting a £1.1m overspend, with a new high-cost placement that was not anticipated at budget setting driving the pressure. Additionally, the Children's Home project has slipped past its planned opening date, meaning budgeted cost avoidance and income benefits will not materialise as planned. The service is reviewing commissioning arrangements but results are uncertain.
findings.matters: Placement costs are volatile and driven by individual cases. A single unanticipated high-cost placement suggests either forecasting weakness or genuine demand volatility that cannot be predicted, creating budget risk.
findings.figures: £1.1m forecast overspend; Children's Home opening delayed beyond Q1 forecast
findings.quote: The children's placements budget is forecasting an overspend of £1.1m, primarily driven by a new high-cost placement that was not anticipated at the time the 2026/27 budget was set.

findings.headline: £15.5m accumulated DSG deficit with no confirmed government funding for 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.detail: The in-year Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast at £5.4m. Combined with the £10.068m brought forward, this creates a £15.452m accumulated deficit equivalent to 10.1% of the council's revised net revenue budget. The council must continue to cash-flow this deficit, but government has not confirmed how DSG deficits will be funded going forward. A recovery plan has been submitted and the council expects an announcement in autumn, but this is conditional.
findings.matters: A £15.5m contingent liability that must be cash-flowed represents a material financial risk. Dependency on future government funding decisions creates uncertainty about the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £5.4m in-year deficit forecast, £15.452m accumulated deficit, 10.1% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: Government has not yet confirmed how DSG deficits will be funded for 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Report No. 57.2026 - 2025-26 Financial Outturn Report, 09/06/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Early debt repayment of £4.5m at 6.69% average rate; no new borrowing undertaken
findings.detail: The council repaid £4.5m of PWLB debt during the year at an average rate of 6.69%, with breakage costs of £0.5m, using investment balances. This reduced the debt portfolio from the budgeted position and resulted in net General Fund savings of £0.2m per annum from lower interest costs. No new borrowing was undertaken.
findings.matters: The council is actively managing down its debt position and maintaining an under-borrowed position (£4.2m under the Capital Financing Requirement). This is positive but requires sustained investment capacity.

findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council repaid a further £4.5m of loan debt at an average rate of 6.69% with breakage costs of £0.5m using investment balances.

findings.paper_title: Report No. 57.2026 - 2025-26 Financial Outturn Report, 09/06/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Treasury achieved 4.42% investment return vs 3.98% benchmark but dependent on £10.1m DSG deficit held in cash rather than invested
findings.detail: Strong treasury performance with £2.5m investment income (vs £2.0m budget) achieved 4.42% average return on £51.5m average investment balances. However, the council cash-flowed the £10.1m DSG accumulated deficit during the year, reducing investment balances and foregoing approximately £0.5m of interest income that would otherwise have supported council services.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is not only a spending pressure but also an opportunity cost burden, reducing available revenue from treasury activities. As the deficit grows further, this foregone income increases.
findings.figures: £2.5m investment income vs £2.0m budget; 4.42% actual vs 3.98% benchmark return; £51.5m average investment balance; £10.1m DSG held in cash; estimated £0.5m foregone interest
